post_message: With 43 newly confirmed infections, U.S. measles cases have reached 2,073 as of Friday. Among all patients, 6% have needed to be hospitalized and 93% have been unvaccinated or have an unknown vaccination status.  Vaccines are the best protection against the disease, which not only can cause severe complications soon after exposure but can also generally weaken the immune system, causing it to "forget" how to fight infections and leaving children highly vulnerable. 💧 On #WorldEnvironmentDay, we focus on the many ways the environment supports global health, from the air we breathe to the water we drink.   A study in Nature earlier this year, for example, predicted that extreme weather events — such as floods that allow mosquito proliferation — could lead to 123 million additional malaria cases in Africa between 2024 and 2050, with 532,000 additional deaths.   While new vaccines are helping, reducing malaria and other diseases requires understanding the environment around us as well.

"I dream of a world where everyone has equal access to both the practice of science and the benefits of science."  2026 Sabin Rising Star Awardee Dr. Senjuti Saha of the Child Health Research Foundation (CHRF) has already left a permanent mark on public health. Her landmark studies on #typhoid epidemiology and antimicrobial resistance formed the scientific foundation for the October 2025 launch of Bangladesh's typhoid conjugate vaccine campaign, where over 40 million children under the age of 15 have been vaccinated so far.  We are proud to have celebrated her accomplishments at the Sabin Awards Ceremony this month. Watch the full recording online at the link in our bio.

Senegal was one of the first countries in Africa to make the switch from pentavalent + polio vaccine to the hexavalent vaccine. The hexavalent vaccine offers protection against more diseases in a single shot, allowing  for a more efficient, streamlined immunization process.  Hear key takeaways about making a successful transition from Dr. Ousseynou Badiane, who manages Senegal's essential program on immunization (EPI) and shared his experiences with others at the Sabin-led Hexavalent Early Adopters workshop for countries transitioning to hexavalent vaccines.

Did you know? 💭 Vaccines are more than an essential public health intervention. They're also a benefit to the economy.  Research shows that in 73 low- and middle-income countries, for every $1 spent on vaccination, there is a $21 return on investment from savings in health care costs, lost wages, and productivity.

Sabin's Boost Community recently concluded the BoostHER webinar series, a three-part global virtual dialogue spotlighting women’s leadership in immunization and advancing gender-responsive practice across the sector. 🙌  Some key takeaways from these essential conversations:  🔹 Say yes before you feel ready. Women often hold themselves back waiting to feel fully prepared. Stepping into opportunities and learning on the job is how careers accelerate. 🔹 Leadership is a practice, not a position. Regardless of title or role, everyone leads daily through how they show up, communicate, and support others. 🔹 Build a team of mentors, not just one. Different mentors serve different needs. Identify gaps in your skills and goals and find people who speak to each. 🔹 Adaptability is a core leadership skill. The only constant in global health is change. The ability to pivot, learn, and stay flexible determines long-term effectiveness. 🔹 Support other women intentionally. Open doors, make introductions, and lift others up. Collective advancement is a leadership responsibility, not just a personal choice. 🔹 See the full conversation online: https://ow.ly/sbSA50Z9VXv  For even more insights, join the Boost Community — more than 5,000 immunization professionals strong, connecting from around the globe ⤵️ https://ow.ly/xVAl50Z9VXu

Marburg virus disease, a deadly hemorrhagic fever related to Ebola, has a fatality rate of up to 88%.  Sabin's cAd3-Marburg Vaccine was administered to more than 2,230 participants in Phase 2 clinical trials in an outbreak setting in Rwanda (2024) and Ethiopia (2025). Sabin team members Elisabeth Wilhelm (left) and Theresa Sommers, PhD, MPH (second from right, back row) met with research partners from the Philippines at UNICEF’s 4th International Social and Behavior Change Communication (SBCC) Summit in Panama last week. The researchers presented findings on social and behavioral communications used in their study of  two geographically isolated and disadvantaged barangays in General Tinio, Nueva Ecija.   Their research is featured in the new compendium, “Social and Behaviour Change to Improve Uptake of Routine Immunization,” from UNICEF, the Sabin Vaccine Institute, and Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance.
